node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Unit of observation
node.description: Identify the individual person, object, event or case from which one row or record of data is collected.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Variable of interest
node.description: Identify the attribute or measurement being collected to answer a statistical question.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Target population
node.description: Identify the full group about which a statistical question or conclusion is intended.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Sampling frame
node.description: Identify the accessible list or source from which a sample is actually selected, and compare it with the target population.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Census versus sample
node.description: Distinguish collecting data from every member of a population from collecting data from a selected subset.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Convenience sampling
node.description: Recognise samples chosen because they are easy to access and explain why they may be biased.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Voluntary response sampling
node.description: Recognise samples made from people who choose to respond and explain why strong opinions may be overrepresented.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Simple random sample procedure
node.description: Use a random mechanism so every member of the sampling frame has an equal chance of selection.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Systematic sampling introduction
node.description: Select every kth member from an ordered list after choosing a starting point, while considering possible ordering bias.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Stratified sampling introduction
node.description: Divide a population into meaningful groups and sample from each group to improve representation.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Cluster sampling introduction
node.description: Select naturally occurring groups or clusters, then collect data from members of selected clusters.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Nonresponse bias
node.description: Recognise bias caused when selected participants do not respond and their responses may differ from those who do respond.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Leading question bias
node.description: Identify survey wording that pushes respondents toward a particular answer.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Double-barrelled question
node.description: Identify survey questions that ask about two ideas at once and therefore make responses hard to interpret.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Ambiguous response options
node.description: Detect response choices that overlap, omit possibilities or use unclear category boundaries.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Balanced response scale
node.description: Design response scales that give balanced options across agreement, frequency or intensity.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Pilot survey questions
node.description: Test survey questions on a small group to find confusing wording, missing choices or recording problems before full data collection.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Anonymous response considerations
node.description: Explain when anonymous responses may reduce social-pressure bias and support ethical data collection.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Measurement unit consistency
node.description: Use consistent units and measurement methods when collecting numerical data.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Data recording protocol
node.description: Define how data will be recorded so repeated observations use the same categories, units and rules.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Repeated measurement reliability
node.description: Use repeated measurements or observations to check consistency and reduce accidental recording error.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Observational versus experimental data
node.description: Distinguish data collected by observing existing conditions from data collected after deliberately changing or controlling a condition.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Controlled variable introduction
node.description: Recognise a condition kept the same during an experiment so that differences can be linked more clearly to the variable being changed.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Treatment condition introduction
node.description: Identify the condition or intervention being compared in a simple experiment.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Observation protocol
node.description: Set rules for what counts as an observed event or behaviour before recording observational data.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Target population defines claim scope
node.description: A statistical claim should only generalise to the population the sampling method reasonably represents.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Sampling frame may miss population members
node.description: A sampling frame that excludes part of the target population can create coverage bias.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Leading questions create response bias
node.description: Survey wording can influence answers and systematically bias the collected data.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Random does not mean haphazard
node.description: A random sample uses a planned chance mechanism, not arbitrary or careless selection.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Experiment changes a condition observation does not
node.description: In an experiment, a condition is deliberately changed or controlled; in an observation, existing conditions are recorded.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Random sample means any sample
node.description: Learner treats any casually chosen sample as random because it was not carefully planned.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Convenient sample is representative
node.description: Learner assumes an easy-to-access group represents the full population without checking selection bias.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Survey wording has no effect
node.description: Learner assumes respondents would answer the same way regardless of leading, confusing or unbalanced wording.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Sampling frame equals population
node.description: Learner assumes the list used for sampling perfectly matches the target population without checking exclusions or duplicates.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Observation proves causation
node.description: Learner treats observational data as proving that one variable caused another without experimental control.

edge.rationale: Identifying the target population directly practises population and sample reasoning.
Stratified sampling is one important sampling method within sampling and representativeness.
Recognising leading questions directly improves survey data collection quality.
A consistent recording protocol is central to reliable data collection.
Controlling variables is a key idea in experimental data collection.
Identifying the unit of observation depends on knowing what data would answer the question.
edge.failure_signal: Learner mixes individuals, responses and variables as if they are the same thing.

edge.rationale: Identifying the variable of interest depends on recognising what kind of data is being collected.
edge.failure_signal: Learner cannot name the attribute or measurement being recorded.

edge.rationale: A refined statistical question identifies the group the question is about.
edge.failure_signal: Learner makes a general claim without specifying the group it applies to.

edge.rationale: A sampling frame can only be judged by comparing it with the intended target population.
edge.failure_signal: Learner assumes the available list exactly matches the group of interest.

edge.rationale: Census and sample distinctions require a defined population.
edge.failure_signal: Learner cannot tell whether data came from everyone or from a subset.

edge.rationale: Convenience sampling is judged by comparing who is easy to access with the sampling frame or target population.
edge.failure_signal: Learner overlooks who was excluded by the easy-access method.

edge.rationale: Voluntary response is a specific non-random selection method with self-selection bias.
edge.failure_signal: Learner treats people who choose to answer as representative of everyone.

edge.rationale: A simple random sample requires a defined sampling frame to choose from.
edge.failure_signal: Learner says a sample is random without defining who could be selected.

edge.rationale: Systematic sampling is easier to evaluate after understanding planned selection methods and random starts.
edge.failure_signal: Learner ignores ordering bias when selecting every kth member.

edge.rationale: Stratified sampling is designed to improve representation of important subgroups.
edge.failure_signal: Learner samples from only one subgroup and calls it representative.

edge.rationale: Cluster sampling requires understanding that a population can be accessed through naturally occurring groups.
edge.failure_signal: Learner confuses clusters with strata or individual random samples.

edge.rationale: Nonresponse bias arises when selected survey participants do not provide responses.
edge.failure_signal: Learner ignores missing responses when judging survey reliability.

edge.rationale: Leading-question bias is a survey-design issue.
edge.failure_signal: Learner accepts loaded wording as neutral.

edge.rationale: Both topics involve evaluating whether question wording distorts or obscures responses.
edge.failure_signal: Learner does not notice that one response must answer two questions at once.

edge.rationale: Clear response options build on clear category labels and non-overlapping categories.
edge.failure_signal: Learner creates overlapping or incomplete answer choices.

edge.rationale: Balanced scales require first recognising clear and complete response options.
edge.failure_signal: Learner writes response scales that favour one side of an opinion.

edge.rationale: Piloting checks whether the wording and response scale work as intended.
edge.failure_signal: Learner launches a survey without testing whether respondents understand the questions.

edge.rationale: Anonymity is part of ethical planning and can affect response honesty.
edge.failure_signal: Learner collects sensitive data without considering privacy or response pressure.

edge.rationale: Consistent measurement units apply when collecting numerical data.
edge.failure_signal: Learner mixes centimetres and metres or different measurement methods without noting it.

edge.rationale: Recording protocols specify consistent units, categories and rules.
edge.failure_signal: Learner records equivalent responses in inconsistent forms.

edge.rationale: Repeated measurements must use the same protocol to reveal reliability rather than procedure changes.
edge.failure_signal: Learner repeats measurements but changes the method each time.

edge.rationale: Observational and experimental data are distinct modes of data collection.
edge.failure_signal: Learner treats any data collection as an experiment.

edge.rationale: Controlled variables are meaningful after distinguishing experiments from observations.
edge.failure_signal: Learner claims a causal comparison without controlling relevant conditions.

edge.rationale: A treatment or condition is interpreted within an experiment where other variables may be controlled.
edge.failure_signal: Learner cannot identify what condition is being compared in the experiment.

edge.rationale: Observation protocols make observational data collection consistent.
edge.failure_signal: Learner records behaviours inconsistently because observation rules were not defined.
